title: Metric Space Topology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Metric Space Topology curriculum: metric space axioms and examples, open/closed sets, convergence of sequences, completeness, compactness, connectedness, and continuity of functions between metric spaces.

questions.question: A metric d on a set X must satisfy which of the following for all x, y, z ∈ X?
options: d(x,y) ≥ 0 with equality iff x=y; d(x,y)=d(y,x); and the triangle inequality d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y)+d(y,z)
d(x,y) = d(y,x) only, with no other requirement
questions.correct_answer: d(x,y) ≥ 0 with equality iff x=y; d(x,y)=d(y,x); and the triangle inequality d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y)+d(y,z)
questions.explanation: These are the three defining axioms of a metric: non-negativity/identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.

questions.question: The usual (Euclidean) metric on ℝ is given by d(x,y) =
questions.correct_answer: |x − y|
questions.explanation: The standard metric on the real line is the absolute value of the difference, which satisfies all metric axioms.

questions.question: The discrete metric on a set X is defined by d(x,y) = 0 if x = y and d(x,y) = 1 otherwise. Under this metric, every subset of X is:
questions.correct_answer: Both open and closed
questions.explanation: In the discrete metric, every singleton {x} is open (it is a ball of radius less than 1), so every subset (a union of singletons) is open, and hence also closed as the complement of an open set.

questions.question: In a metric space (X, d), the open ball B(x0, r) is defined as:
questions.correct_answer: {x ∈ X : d(x, x0) < r}
questions.explanation: The open ball centered at x0 with radius r consists of all points strictly closer to x0 than r.

questions.question: A subset U of a metric space X is called open if:
options: For every point x ∈ U, there exists r > 0 such that B(x, r) ⊆ U
U contains all its limit points
U equals the whole space X
questions.correct_answer: For every point x ∈ U, there exists r > 0 such that B(x, r) ⊆ U
questions.explanation: Openness means every point of U has some open ball around it entirely contained within U.

questions.question: A subset F of a metric space X is called closed if:
options: Its complement X \ F is open
It is always a finite set
questions.correct_answer: Its complement X \ F is open
questions.explanation: By definition, a closed set is one whose complement in X is an open set.

questions.question: Which of the following is true of arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets in a metric space?
options: Both arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open
Only unions are open; intersections are never open
Only finite intersections are open; unions are never open
Neither unions nor intersections of open sets are open
questions.correct_answer: Both arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open
questions.explanation: This is a fundamental topological property: any union of open sets is open, and any finite intersection of open sets is also open.

questions.question: A point x is called a limit point (accumulation point) of a set A in a metric space if:
options: Every open ball around x contains a point of A different from x
questions.correct_answer: Every open ball around x contains a point of A different from x
questions.explanation: A limit point is one that can be approximated arbitrarily closely by other points of A, distinct from x itself.

questions.question: A set A in a metric space is closed if and only if:
options: A contains all of its limit points
questions.correct_answer: A contains all of its limit points
questions.explanation: A classical characterization: a set is closed precisely when it contains every point that is a limit of points from within the set.

questions.question: A sequence (xn) in a metric space (X, d) converges to x if:
questions.correct_answer: d(xn, x) → 0 as n → ∞
questions.explanation: Convergence in a metric space means the distance between the sequence terms and the limit point shrinks to zero.

questions.question: In a metric space, the limit of a convergent sequence, if it exists, is:
options: Equal to the diameter of the space
questions.correct_answer: Unique
questions.explanation: Using the triangle inequality, one can show that a sequence in a metric space cannot converge to two distinct limits.

questions.question: A sequence (xn) in a metric space is called a Cauchy sequence if:
options: For every ε > 0, there exists N such that d(xm, xn) < ε for all m, n > N
questions.correct_answer: For every ε > 0, there exists N such that d(xm, xn) < ε for all m, n > N
questions.explanation: The Cauchy condition requires terms to become arbitrarily close to each other, not merely to a specific limit.

questions.question: A metric space (X, d) is called complete if:
options: Every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point in X
Every sequence in X is bounded
X has only finitely many points
questions.correct_answer: Every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point in X
questions.explanation: Completeness means there are no 'missing' limit points — every Cauchy sequence actually converges within the space.

questions.question: Which of the following metric spaces is NOT complete?
options: The rational numbers ℚ with the usual metric
The real numbers ℝ with the usual metric
questions.correct_answer: The rational numbers ℚ with the usual metric
questions.explanation: ℚ is not complete because Cauchy sequences of rationals can converge to irrational numbers (e.g. approximations of √2), which lie outside ℚ.

questions.question: Every convergent sequence in a metric space is necessarily:
questions.correct_answer: A Cauchy sequence
questions.explanation: If a sequence converges to a limit x, its terms become arbitrarily close to x, and hence arbitrarily close to each other, satisfying the Cauchy condition.

questions.question: A subset K of a metric space X is called compact if:
options: Every open cover of K has a finite subcover
questions.correct_answer: Every open cover of K has a finite subcover
questions.explanation: This is the general (Heine-Borel style) topological definition of compactness in terms of open covers.

questions.question: The Heine-Borel Theorem states that a subset of ℝ^n (with the usual metric) is compact if and only if it is:
questions.correct_answer: Closed and bounded
questions.explanation: In Euclidean space ℝ^n, compactness is precisely equivalent to being both closed and bounded, a special case not true in general metric spaces.

questions.question: Every compact metric space is necessarily:
questions.correct_answer: Complete
questions.explanation: Compactness implies completeness: any Cauchy sequence in a compact space has a convergent subsequence, which forces the whole sequence to converge.

questions.question: The open interval (0, 1) with the usual metric on ℝ is:
options: Not compact, since it is bounded but not closed in ℝ
questions.correct_answer: Not compact, since it is bounded but not closed in ℝ
questions.explanation: Although bounded, (0,1) fails to be closed (it does not contain its limit points 0 and 1), so by Heine-Borel it is not compact; it is also not complete as a metric space in its own right.

questions.question: A metric space X is called connected if:
options: X cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets
Every subset of X is open
questions.correct_answer: X cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets
questions.explanation: Connectedness means there is no way to 'split' the space into two separate open pieces; such a split is called a disconnection.

questions.question: A subset of ℝ with the usual metric is connected if and only if it is:
options: An interval (including degenerate ones like a single point)
questions.correct_answer: An interval (including degenerate ones like a single point)
questions.explanation: In ℝ, the connected subsets are exactly the intervals — sets with no 'gaps' — due to the order structure of the real line.

questions.question: A function f: X → Y between metric spaces is continuous at x0 if:
options: For every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that d_X(x,x0) < δ implies d_Y(f(x), f(x0)) < ε
d_X(x, x0) = d_Y(f(x), f(x0)) for all x
questions.correct_answer: For every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that d_X(x,x0) < δ implies d_Y(f(x), f(x0)) < ε
questions.explanation: This is the metric-space generalization of the epsilon-delta definition of continuity from real analysis.

questions.question: A function f: X → Y between metric spaces is continuous on X if and only if:
options: The preimage of every open set in Y is open in X
The image of every open set in X is open in Y
questions.correct_answer: The preimage of every open set in Y is open in X
questions.explanation: This topological characterization of continuity is equivalent to the epsilon-delta definition and is often more convenient for proofs.

questions.question: If f: X → Y is continuous and K ⊆ X is compact, then f(K) is:
questions.correct_answer: Compact in Y
questions.explanation: Continuous images of compact sets are always compact, a key preservation theorem in metric space topology.

questions.question: If f: X → Y is continuous and X is connected, then f(X) is:
questions.correct_answer: Connected in Y
questions.explanation: Continuous functions preserve connectedness: the continuous image of a connected space is always connected.

questions.question: The interior of a set A in a metric space is defined as:
options: The union of all open sets contained in A
The set of all limit points of A
questions.correct_answer: The union of all open sets contained in A
questions.explanation: The interior int(A) is the largest open set contained within A, consisting of points that have an open ball entirely inside A.

questions.question: The closure of a set A in a metric space is defined as:
options: The intersection of all closed sets containing A (equivalently, A together with its limit points)
questions.correct_answer: The intersection of all closed sets containing A (equivalently, A together with its limit points)
questions.explanation: The closure of A is the smallest closed set containing A, obtained by adding all of A's limit points.

questions.question: A subset A of a metric space X is called dense in X if:
options: The closure of A equals X
A = X exactly, with no closure needed
questions.correct_answer: The closure of A equals X
questions.explanation: Density means every point of X can be approximated arbitrarily well by points of A; e.g. ℚ is dense in ℝ.

questions.question: Two metrics d1 and d2 on a set X are called equivalent if:
options: They induce the same open sets (the same topology) on X
d1(x,y) = d2(x,y) for all x, y
One of them is always zero
They have different completeness properties by definition
questions.correct_answer: They induce the same open sets (the same topology) on X
questions.explanation: Equivalent metrics may differ numerically but generate identical notions of open sets, convergence, and continuity.

questions.question: The distance function d(x, y) = |x1 − y1| + |x2 − y2| on ℝ² (the taxicab/Manhattan metric) is:
options: Not a valid metric because it can be negative
The same as the Euclidean metric numerically
Undefined for points with negative coordinates
questions.correct_answer: A valid metric on ℝ²
questions.explanation: The taxicab metric satisfies all three metric axioms (non-negativity, symmetry, triangle inequality), making it a legitimate alternative metric on ℝ².
